Not so. Plato meant to portray is that the best ruler is one that is a philosopher. I'm torn on this issue, and I apologize if I am resurrecting a dead thread but Boats is showing this as only 32 minutes old (comments say otherwise). It seems pretty clear that some fields of philosophy, such as metaphysics and logic, are indeed the kinds of fields that require rigorous training before one can even begin to comment. Others, such as language and ethics, have the potential to be something everyone contributes to. Working in ethics, I often question my arguments with intuitons I get from friends and family, and try to understand how those intuitons fit into a broader picture. Even if this is involving people in a very limited way, I believe we should avoid making philosophy any more of a private conversation than it already is.

Exactly why I disagree with the article (well, other than the way that Kant was represented). Philosophy isn't a tool we use to accomplish some end, like biochemistry or physics. It's the thing that chooses our ends for us, and furthermore, it demands more of its audience. A person could live a perfectly fulfilling live without knowing a thing about orbital mechanics; the same is not true about philosophy. Even if it's not quite academic philosophy, even if it's not what you or I would even call proper philosophy, at some point, a person who wants a rich life is going to have to ask themselves "Why am I working towards?"

These two different institutions are often mistakenly used interchangeably when their purposes are very different. The definitions that I present are those used in the American criminal justice system and may be different for other countries.

Jail: Incarceration for a period under a year. Used for holding people who've committed misdemeanor offenses.

Prison: Incarceration for a year or more. Used for holding people who've committed a felony offense or multiple misdemeanor offenses.

The difference? Other than the time in which a criminal has to sit in a cell, the biggest difference is the severity of the crimes committed. These definitions provide a mechanism of separating offenders based on their tendency to violence. You're not going to find a petty one-time shoplifter sharing a cell with a convicted mass murderer.
